flashcard_questions.q: What is promotion in the marketing mix?
flashcard_questions.a: Reminding, informing or persuading customers to buy a product or service.
Paying to have a brand associated with an individual, event or team.
A temporary offering that lets consumers test a product before a full launch.
Promoting a product through a distinctive name, design or image.
Using social networks to spread a marketing message quickly from person to person.
A marketing email sent to customers who have signed up to receive it.
The combination of promotional methods a business uses to reach its target market.
Using data about a customer's browsing behaviour to display relevant adverts.

flashcard_questions.q: What advantage do magazine adverts have over newspaper adverts?
flashcard_questions.a: Magazines have a pass-on readership, so several people read one copy.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is television advertising unsuitable for most start-ups?
flashcard_questions.a: It is too expensive for a small business.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can special offers damage a business's profit?
flashcard_questions.a: Each item sells for less, so margins shrink.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main risk of sponsoring a celebrity?
Which football club did JD Sports sponsor to reach 16–24 year olds?
Which supermarket runs Home Panels where selected customers test new products?
What percentage sales boost did the Old Spice viral campaign achieve?

notes: 15 cards: 8 term→definition (promotion, sponsorship, product trial, branding, viral advertising, e-newsletter, promotional mix, targeted online advertising), 4 single-fact advantage/disadvantage cards (magazines, TV cost, special offers, celebrity risk), 3 concept→named example (JD Sports/Bournemouth, Tesco Home Panels, Old Spice 60%). Dropped the Bentley premium-price example to stay at 15 — branding is already covered by the definition card.
